name: Banawá
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [Everett 1995: 329] (138) Acentuação: É um sistema trocaico, com os pés construidos da esquerda para a direita, sobre moras. A acentuação principal recai sobre a última sílaba acentuada, indicando a presença de um pé binário não iterativo, com núcleo à direita (isto é, um pé iâmbico) à margem direita da palavra. || [Everett 1996: 22] As originally described in BBE, Banawá stresses every other mora from left-to-right within the word, skipping word-initial vowels in words with more than two syllables. The words in (46) illustrate the basic stress rule: (46) a. súirì 'penis' b. wárabù 'ear' c. wánakàri 'spider' d. yífuyà 'fire' e. uwárià 'one' f. úwi 'cry' ... i. dábikàri 'bee'
new_statements.translation: [Everett 1995: 329] (138) Stress: It is a trochaic system, with feet built from left to right over moras. Main stress falls on the last stressed syllable, indicating the presence of a non-iterative binary foot, right-headed (i.e. an iambic foot), at the right margin of the word.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked under (1) Everett 1995 'Sistemas prosódicos da família Arawá' (Wetzels ed.), pdf p.170 = book pp.328-329: I viewed the page image and the scanned text. Under '3.6 Madi / 3.6.1 Banawá' the printed text reads exactly: '(138) Acentuação: É um sistema trocaico, com os pés construidos da esquerda para a direita, sobre moras. A acentuação principal recai sobre a última sílaba acentuada, indicando a presença de um pé binário não iterativo, com núcleo à direita (isto é, um pé iâmbico) à margem direita da palavra.' -- verbatim as quoted (the scanned txt has tilde artefacts only). The section opens 'Em Buller, Buller e Everett (1993), o sistema prosódico do Banawá é descrito detalhadame…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress every odd-numbered mora counting from the left (left-to-right moraic trochees; syllables CV, CVV, a foot may split CVV); a word-initial onsetless vowel is skipped in words of more than two moras, so V-initial words stress even-numbered moras (enéki, abébirì); odd mora counts leave a stressed degenerate final foot (mákarì/màkarí). Which beat is primary is disputed: Everett 1995 says the last stressed syllable; Everett 1996a/b's transcriptions and Hyde 2007 (from Buller, Buller & Everett 1993) make the penultimate stress primary (wánakàri, báburùru, mètuwásimà, kèrewéduàma, tìnarífabùne), i.e. initial primary in 2-4-mora CV-initial words, third-mora primary in 5-6-mora words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: All other foot heads carry secondary stress: rhythmic alternation on every other mora across the whole word, including a word-final degenerate (monomoraic) foot in odd-parity words; Ladefoged, Ladefoged & Everett found no final lengthening (Everett 1996: 4.4.3.1).
new_statements.exceptions: Word-initial onsetless V unfooted/unstressed except in bimoraic words (ába 'fish', áwa, áwi are trochaic); monosyllables lengthen to satisfy the bimoraic minimal word (fáa 'water', bíi, búu); masculine suffix -i (word-final post-vocalic i) is never stressed/extrametrical (káwiè-i, kíe-i); truncated names/vocatives take iambic 'Vocative Stress'; auxiliary+verb form one prosodic word (réukàna); Hyde 2007: 274 reports that BBE 1993 mention 'a number of unexplained exceptions' to the primary-stress placement; Everett's own primary/secondary diacritics are inconsistent (mákarì (69e) vs màkarí 4.4.3.1 in ROA-121) and Everett 1995 vs 1996 disagree on whether the last or the penultimate beat is primary.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prosodic word = lexical word plus clitic-like auxiliary combinations); data are isolated citation forms and words from texts; stress placement 'confirmed instrumentally' on isolated words from six men recorded with P. & J. Ladefoged in 1995 (Everett 1996: 6; LLE 1997).
new_statements.identity_note: bana1306 is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO 639-3 code [bnh], merged in 2007 into Madi [jaa] (Glottolog jama1261). All sources found describe the Banawá dialect (Glottolog bana1307) of Madi, spoken on the Banawá river, Amazonas, Brazil (c. 80-100 speakers; fieldwork by E. & B. Buller (SIL) and D. Everett; recordings by P. & J. Ladefoged 1995). Everett (1995: sec. 3.6 'Madi') and Dixon treat Banawá, Jamamadí and Jarawara as dialects of one language; note that the Jarawara dialect's stress is described differently (trochees built right-to-left, main stress penultimate) in Everett 1995: 330, so a Madi-level catalog entry should not silently merge the two dialects.

new_statements.quote: Banawá displays quantity-insensitive rhythmic stress on alternating vowels. In the presence of more than one stress, the penultimate stress is realized as primary. In consonant-initial (C-initial) words, stress falls on alternating vowels, starting from the first one. [...] In vowel-initial (V-initial) words with three or more vowels, stress falls on alternating vowels, but in this case the first vowel to be stressed is the second one. In V-initial words with two vowels, stress falls on the first vowel (á.ba 'fish', ú.wi 'cry'). [p.170] || In Banawá, primary stress never falls on the final mora [p.173]
new_statements.citation: Martínez-Paricio, Violeta & René Kager. 2020. A note on the relationship between grid structure and metrical structure in Banawá. Linguistic Inquiry 51(1): 168-183. doi:10.1162/ling_a_00334
new_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Banawá Stress Data', p.170 (PDF p.5); also p.173 (PDF p.8) sec. 3.1 and fn. 3 p.171 (PDF p.6)
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Everett 1995 statement that stress is rhythmic, built from the left on moras (Everett: trochaic feet L-to-R on moras; M-P&K: alternating vowels from the left, quantity-insensitive at the mora level), but CONTRADICTS Everett 1995 (138) on primary-stress placement: Everett 1995 puts main stress on the last stressed syllable ('A acentuação principal recai sobre a última sílaba acentuada'), whereas M-P&K p.170 say 'the penultimate stress is realized as primary' and p.173 'primary stress never falls on the final mora'. On this point M-P&K side with BBE 1993, Everett 1996 (ROA-121, the second existing quote: acute on the first stressed mora in 2-foot words, the middle one…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Rhythmic (alternating) stress counted on vowels/morae from the left, ignoring syllable weight and even cutting across heavy CVV syllables: in C-initial words the 1st, 3rd, 5th.. vowel is stressed; in V-initial words of three or more vowels the 2nd, 4th.. vowel is stressed; V-initial bimoraic words stress the first vowel (ába, úwi). Where there is more than one stress, the penultimate stress is primary (e.g. má.ka.rì, bà.dué.bi.rì, kè.re.wé.duà.ma, a.tì.keí.ja.rì.ne); primary stress never falls on the final mora. The authors analyse this as left-to-right moraic iambs with a moraic word-initial onset, but the surface placement is the same as in BBE 1993.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: every non-primary rhythmic beat is secondary (marked with grave accents, e.g. bá.bu.rù.ru, kèi.já.ri.nè, tìa.sía.nì); secondary stress may fall on a word-final mora (sú.kià) but word-final /i/ after a vowel (the masculine suffix) is never stressed (fn. 3, p.171, after BBE 1993:285).
new_statements.exceptions: V-initial two-vowel words stress the first vowel (ába, úwi), which the authors treat as a final rhythmic reversal; post-vocalic word-final /i/ never stressed and assumed unfooted; long vowels largely restricted to monosyllables (bíi, háa) and treated as underlyingly short; no CV words. No lexical exceptions reported. All data is second-hand from BBE 1993, Everett 1996/1997 and Ladefoged, Ladefoged & Everett 1997.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper describes Banawá as 'an endangered Arawan language spoken in the Brazilian Amazon' using only second-hand data from Buller, Buller & Everett 1993, Everett 1996/1997 and Ladefoged, Ladefoged & Everett 1997 (the SIL Porto Velho / UCLA 1995 material). Glottolog bana1306 is a bookkeeping code (retired ISO bnh); the same variety is the Banawá dialect bana1307 of Madi/Jamamadí (jama1261). Footnote 2 cites Jarawara (Dixon 2004), 'a closely related dialect mutually intelligible with Banawá', only for the existence of V-initial and VV-initial words, not for stress.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, on primary-stress placement only. Everett 1995 (Sistemas prosódicos, p.329 (138), the catalog's existing statement) says the main stress falls on the LAST stressed syllable (final foot). Martínez-Paricio & Kager 2020 p.170 say the PENULTIMATE stress is primary and p.173 that primary stress never falls on the final mora; this agrees with Buller, Buller & Everett 1993, with Everett 1996 ROA-121 (acute on the first stressed mora of two-foot words, e.g. wánakàri, dábikàri, and the middle one of three-foot words, kèrewéduàma) and with Hyde 2007 ('the primary stress is the penultimate stress'). The StressTyp2 editors' note (the StressTyp2 entry for this language) records the same split between BBE 1993 and the Everett 1995 ms. All sources agree on the rhythmic alternation from the left on moras, the skipping of the initial vowel in V-initial words of three or more vowels, and unstressed word-final post-vocalic -i. The weight of sources (BBE 1993 primary description, Everett 1996, Hyde 2007, M-P&K 2020) favours penultimate-stress-as-primary over Everett 1995's final-foot statement.

sources.note: Sec. 3.6.1 Banawá, p.329 (138): trochaic system, feet built left-to-right on moras; main stress falls on the last stressed syllable; p.330 (142): word-initial V and word-final post-vocalic i are extrametrical (suspendable for minimality); minimal word = one bimoraic foot; a foot may split a CVV syllable. Explicitly a summary of Buller, Buller & Everett 1993. Also p.330: Jarawara dialect is trochaic right-to-left with penultimate main stress; p.333: Banawá, Paumarí, Dení keep the proto-Arawá left-to-right trochaic system.
